items.title: Heat 108, Knicks 105: “Really tough to win a poorly coached, corruptly reffed, half rotation injured game.”
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks (12-7) lost two Emirates NBA Cup games this season but defeated the Cavaliers on Wednesday. Their chances of reaching the next round and continuing their defense of the Cup weren’t nonexistent, but they needed to beat the Heat (11-7) by more than six points and for the Pacers to drop the Sixers.

First things first: the surging Heat are a handful even when New York’s roster is complete. The Knicks had to meet the challenge without OG Anunoby (calf), Andre Drummond (concussion), Miles McBride (groin), and Jordan Clarkson (foot). The remaining players weren’t altogether healthy, either: Karl-Anthony Towns (19 PTS, 10 RBS, 34 MIN) has an abdominal contusion, and Josh Hart (6 PTS, 9 RBS, 8 AST) is playing through a sore knee and shoulder. Our depleted Knickerbockers fell behind in the first quarter, then went down by 23 in the second. They cut their deficit to five in the third frame and had the Heat on the ropes in crunch time. A few missed free throws, an uncalled flagrant foul, and odd coaching decisions let the rally—and their Cup dreams—slip through their fingers. Final score: 108-105.

Quoth DWLLTheKnicksfan: “Really tough to win a poorly coached, corruptly reffed, half rotation injured game. Respect that it was close.”

After the Knicks fell behind 15-7, coach Mike Brown replaced Hart with Pacôme Dadiet (4 PTS, 1 STL, 21 MIN, +7). Pac-Man played arm-flapping defense that disrupted the flow and led to a Miami turnover, then dunked a Brunson pass on the run. We’re starting to see the vision! The French fella stayed on the floor when the next round of swaps came, playing alongside Brunson, Hart, Jose Alvarado (7 PTS, 15 MIN), and James Wiseman (11 PTS). The latter lasted just two minutes and committed a foul that heralded the return of Towns. Not a great first look on a night when Drummond was out.

New York logged nine boards in the first quarter. Giannis Antetokounmpo (22 PTS, 23 RBS, 32 MIN) matched that total alone, scarfing up most of Miami’s 14 boards. A physical game had Towns wincing in pain, and we were wincing at New York’s crappy shooting (2-of-11 from deep). With the Floridians sinking half of their three-pointers, the Knicks trailed 31-21 at the break.

In the second quarter, Mohamed Diawara and the Tylers (Kolek, Nickel) took the floor. Miami scored 12 unanswered while the ’Bockers continued to shoot like the Blind Boys of Alabama. The rookie Nickel looked lost and the coach bewildered. Mike Brown called for time when the score reached 48-27.

Out of that timeout, Brown sent Wiseman and Dadiet back in. Wiseman’s minutes were rough. On consecutive plays, Wiggins picked off his inbound pass for a layup, and then Ryan Conwell intercepted his inbound pass. Unsurprisingly, he suffered a quick hook. Mike was running out of levers to pull as his team fell behind by 23. With four rotation players out and his starters all posting a plus-minus of -13 or worse, the coach fielded 11 different players in the first half in an attempt to slow Erik Spoelstra’s squad, which scored inside, outside, and wherever else it wanted.

Thanks to a spirited late-half nine-oh run, the home team entered halftime trailing 60-44. There was plenty of blame to go around for our heroes. Towns (still painin’!) and Brunson combined for 25 of their team’s 44 points, but the other starters had five points each, and the Knicks’ bench had been outscored by its Miami counterpart, 30-4.

Through the half, the Flamingos shot 45% from the field and 36% from deep (9-of-25), while New York managed 40% and a miserable 21% (4-of-19). The Heat held only slight advantages in rebounds (24-23) and points in the paint (22-18) but were considerably better at protecting the ball. Nine Knicks turnovers yielded 11 Miami points, while the Heat committed just four turnovers that yielded three New York points. Worse, Miami won the battle for second-chance points, 10-0.

Over the first two minutes of the second half, Towns, Bridges, and Shamet combined for nine points to cut the deficit to 61-53. Miami fought back, but New York looked rejuvenated and alert (a marked improvement from the tryptophan blues of the first half). By the midway point of the quarter, the Knicks had converted five straight shots, reducing their deficit to five. As we’ve seen in game after game this season, it takes a lot of energy to climb out of deep holes. As the Knicks faltered, back-to-back Bridges turnovers allowed Giannis and Bam Adebayo (25 PTS, 7 RBS) to hammer Miami’s lead back to 11.

Our heroes got an unexpected lift from Wiseman. He leaped into the fray, scoring seven points on three buckets and a free throw late in the third. That was more like it! Add a Brunson floater and an Antetokounmpo shot-clock violation, and New York trailed 86-79 at the horn.

Bam was a bother to start the fourth, netting two buckets, blocking shots by Shamet and Kolek, and drawing two fouls from Towns. Towns headed to the bench with four fouls at the 8:27 mark. Meanwhile, Shamet, Bridges, and Kolek each contributed layups to keep the Knicks within striking distance. The Heat struggled from the perimeter, with OAKAAKUYOAKs Tim Hardaway Jr. and Bobby Portis blowing opportunities to extend the lead.

Down 91-85 with plenty of game remaining, New York scored seven unanswered points, fueled by the bench mob. Wednesday’s hero, Alvarado, scored five consecutive points, including a step-back three off his own offensive rebound, while Dadiet contributed a steal and a reverse layup off Brunson’s eighth assist to give the Knicks their first lead. Davion Mitchell finally broke Miami’s scoring drought with a floater, putting the Heat ahead 93-92 with six minutes remaining.

At the two-minute mark, the good guys trailed by three points after two freebies by Shamet. From there, Giannis launched an ill-advised, deep airball late in the shot clock; Brunson and Pelle Larsson traded free throws; Hart made one of two at the stripe; and Adebayo made the differential four with 44 seconds left. Captain Clutch’s floater made it 104-102. Giannis missed two free throws with 14 seconds on the clock, and Adebayo fouled Wiseman on the loose ball, giving our heroes a of hope. My bingo card did not have Wiseman shooting free throws with the game on the line. How about yours?

The young journeyman made one, missed one, and Giannis snagged the board and called a timeout. 104-103, 13 seconds to go. When play resumed, Dadiet fouled Mitchell, who made both attempts. On the Knicks’ inbounds play, the ball swung to Brunson in the corner, where he was fouled by Conwell. Even though Conwell violated JB’s landing space, Scott “The Enforcer” Foster deemed it a common foul. Cap made two of three at the line. Spoelstra called a timeout. 106-105, nine seconds.

Larsson got a breakaway dunk—on the exact same inbounds play the Heat had run on their previous possession. Mike Brown elected not to call a timeout, and Brunson missed a contested triple to end the game.

This is your recap, chaps. As for the Knicks, they’ll sleep in their own beds for a few more days and host the Hawks on Sunday. Rest up, troops.

items.title: Game Discussion Thread: Knicks vs. Heat, November 27, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Tonight, the New York Knicks (12-6) host the Miami Heat (10-7) at the World’s Most Famous Arena for their final game of NBA Cup group play. Our heroes have won six straight, most recently dispatching the Cavaliers 121-102 on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the Heat had won seven consecutive games before walking into a 76er buzzsaw. Can the Knicks keep the good times rolling against a retooled Miami squad featuring that hot young Greek talent, Giannis Antetokounmpo?

Will New York’s cup come up empty, or will it runneth over? Find out at 7 p.m. EST on Prime Video. This is your game thread. This is . Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Enjoy yourselves in peace and harmony. And go Knicks!

items.title: How the Knicks can advance in the NBA Cup
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
After the Knicks’ valiant comeback effort at Gainbridge Fieldhouse came up empty on November 13, they fell to 6-6 on the season and 0-2 in NBA Cup play. After an incredible run the year prior to claim the organization’s first trophy of any kind in 27 years (foreshadowing), they seemed fated to become the third consecutive NBA Cup champion to be bounced in the group stage.

Yet, one six-game winning streak and an incredible fourth quarter in a Cup game against the Cavs later, and the Knicks are mathematically alive heading into Black Friday against Giannis Antetokounmpo and the red-hot Miami Heat.

Now, after winning the Treble last year, experiencing the fatigue from last year’s Cup run that led to the 2-9 stretch from hell, and, you know, defending a real championship, a tournament that already had limited interest from Knicks fans seems to have the opposite intended effect, to the point where it might be beneficial to the knockout round altogether.

But the Knicks are currently the only team to have never been grouped in Cup play, and since these games count toward the team’s 82-game record, there’s plenty to play for as the Knicks look to defend the first of their three trophies.

Here’s a look at the current standings in East Group B and the East’s wild card, both of which are still in play:

The simplest path is to win the group, which simply requires two things:

  • to the Heat by in regulation

What helps the Knicks here is their point differential. They lost the games to Philly and Indiana by five and two points respectively, which allowed their 19-point win over Cleveland to put them in a decent spot.

Winning an NBA game by seven is the easy part; relying on an injured and struggling Pacers team to defeat the No. 1 seed in the East is another. Now, the Sixers look like a paper tiger with their clutch reliance (their Cup PD is negative because of this), but this reads like a game that would be a blowout.

The current injury report has Jaylen Brown out with hamstring management and Joel Embiid questionable with an illness for the Sixers, while Tyrese Haliburton, Ben Sheppard, and Johnny Furphy are still out for Indiana. TJ McConnell, Larry Nance Jr., and Kelly Oubre Jr. are questionable.

If the Sixers win, they clinch Group B. If they lose, the Knicks will get a shot at being the first 2-loss NBA Cup group winner in an unlikely five-way tie.

In the event of a Sixers win, things get a lot more complicated.

First of all, the Knicks would need there to be zero 3-1 non-group winners for obvious reasons. That means they’ll need losses from the Hawks, Pistons, and Raptors. Toronto already has a lower point differential, so margin wouldn’t matter there.

Margin would matter with the other two. The Hawks are at +21 and the Pistons are at +31, so the Knicks are going to need to win and win by a lot to guarantee they get in.

The simplest path to a wild card berth in the event of a Sixers win looks like this:

  • Heat by

The margin of victory would likely not need to be that big, as the more the Pistons and Hawks lose by, the more it knocks that down. The absolute minimum the Knicks would have to win by is seven to pass the Heat in point differential, but to only have to win by that much, they’d need the Bucks to win by 13 and the Celtics to win by 3.

Which brings the difficulty aspect. You’re asking two of the worst teams in the league to win games against significantly better teams, one of which is a matchup between a 2-win Bucks team and the reigning No. 1 seed. That’s probably not happening.

Also, there is the spoiler aspect that could theoretically damage both of these scenarios. If the Pacers (-27 PD) or Nets (-11 PD) win by such ridiculous margins, they would have a chance to steal a spot in the knockout round.

Now, personally, a Hali-less Pacers team winning by damn near 50 or the Nets beating the Raptors by 30+ would be pretty stunning, but we’re already asking for stunning things to happen to get this far.

In layman’s terms, a fourth consecutive trip to the knockout round is still unlikely, but possible.

It’ll make for a fun night of scoreboard watching, that’s for sure.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Sometimes your mind or your body just takes a second’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
If you still have leftovers in the fridge, congratulations. That means you’ll be able to celebrate twice today.

First, a Knicks win over the Heat. Then, feasting on another round of reheated turkey, mac and cheese, and mashed potatoes.

Here’s yesterday’s post, slightly padded with a few more quotes.

On the Knicks still having room for improvement:

“I’ve said this before, we play so many games. You can never get too high. I guess we’re 12-3 since the start, but our [performance] does still stink. We haven’t arrived. We still have to embrace the little things.

“They do this (points downward), but eventually they’re going to do this (points upward). When we do that, handling the challenges in front of us the right way is going to be big. You can’t get too high in this league because you’re that close to going the other way. Just like if you’re down, it’s not the end of the world; you’re that close to flipping it. So you try to stay even-keeled and kind of stick with your process, especially if it’s something that you believe in. And we believe in it. Eventually things are going to change or turn in the right direction.”

On Jordan Clarkson being instrumental in establishing the Knicks’ flexible bench rotation and wanting him to remain with the organization beyond his playing career:

“As a coach, you could want to do that, but you have to have others around you that will at least support it initially to see how it turns out. And a huge, huge, huge catalyst for that was Jordan Clarkson. Jordan Clarkson was the one, if you’re talking about giving 100 percent out there to what allows me to do that, I think Jordan Clarkson gave me at least 90 percent of the opportunity to do it, because here’s an accomplished veteran that could be in the rotation for almost any team out there, let alone a championship team, and I can literally play him six straight games and then sit him 10 straight games and he’s gonna be the same dude every fricken’ day. And he’s gonna talk the same way to his teammates. Not ‘can you believe what Mike Brown did?’ Nah, he’s gonna be the same dude, uplift the group, and then when I call his number again, he’s gonna be ready to go. He’s a guy that, even when he gets done playing, it’s one of those things where you hope that he can just be a part of this organization in some way, shape or form until he doesn’t want to be part of this organization. He’s that type of person, in my opinion.”

On the benefits of potentially missing the NBA Cup knockout rounds:

“It is important (to win and potentially advance), but the reality of it is, when you look at the schedule, and you see that our percentage [to advance] is not that high, and so they kind of shared with me what our schedule would look like if we don’t go and if we do go. And you look at it, you’re like, ‘Whoa, that’s a lot of days off if you don’t go.’ And so again, you want to compete; you want to win. But if you don’t, in my opinion, when you look at the schedule… you’re like, there’s an opportunity if you got some guys banged up to get rest and/or to work on some things in between the games that you have if you’re not involved in the Cup.”

On the physical and mental toll of competing in the NBA Cup:

“I didn’t really break it down to an 83rd game, but when I talk about the Cup, it adds a level of stress maybe on your mind and your body because the games are intense as you go along and you’re playing more games in a short amount of time.

“I remember it was like, game, game, game, and then you win the Cup, and you celebrate it that night, and you hop on a plane and go play in Indiana the next night. And so it’s great. You like the competition and the setup, but it adds a lot of stress to you physically and mentally. I’m saying this because especially with the extended season we had last year and how taxing the games were for our playoff run mentally and physically, I’m trying to be smart, so if — knock on wood — we end up advancing, I’ll try to be smart about it.”

On refusing to chase regular-season wins at all costs and learning from Golden State’s 73-win season:

“I try not to chase wins, especially early in the season. You want to win, but I’m not going to win every game at all costs.

“I wasn’t part of the staff [for the first Golden State title] [Golden State] won Steve [Kerr’s] first year. Then they lost in the second year, but they set a regular season record of 73 wins, and one of the things that he used to tell me, they gassed themselves trying to get this record and come playoff time they just didn’t have enough in the tank to close it. And so that always sits right here for me.”

On calling Pacôme Dadiet into his office and threatening to remove him from the rotation over his lack of effort:

“I didn’t think he played hard in the game before. And I actually called him into my office and showed him some film. I told him, ‘As a young guy, if you don’t play hard, I can’t play you.’

“And I said, ‘Believe me, I got a lot of guys I can go to. I’m not afraid to go to somebody else. So the least you could do is play hard.’ And I showed him how he wasn’t. And I thought [Wednesday], he played hard.”

On leaving OG Anunoby’s injury management to the medical staff:

“There are a lot of medical terms that are above my head. They tell me and I don’t really pick up on the injury. If he’s out, I change my minutes sheet. And then I’ll just wait for them to tell me when he’s back. [Wednesday], OG’s individual work happened before shootaround and I didn’t even know he had individual work until his player development guy told me later on. You never want a guy to hurt himself more. But I don’t think about it.”

On the Knicks still having plenty of room for improvement despite winning 12 of their last 15 games:

“We’re 12-3 since the start, but our s–t still does stink. We haven’t arrived, and we still have to embrace the little things.”

On the Knicks never panicking after their 0-3 start and gradually finding their rhythm:

“I don’t think we had any panic. It wasn’t like we started 0 and 3 and we were getting blown out by 15 and 20 every game. It was a possession game each of those three losses and could’ve gone either way. So we knew that, and we knew it was just a play here or a play there that could’ve changed the game. We just tried to make sure we’re focusing on every possession. Sometimes your mind or your body just takes a second at the beginning of the season. I feel like we’re in a good space, physically and mentally, continuing to get better. Really diving into our core principles.”

On Brown experimenting with an unusually deep rotation against Cleveland:

“I looked at the bench in the first quarter and realized, ‘Wow, we played like 10 people in that first quarter.’”

On the Knicks’ supporting cast stepping up and trusting Karl-Anthony Towns and Jalen Brunson as their leaders:

“I mean, it’s big for our team. Those guys [Towns and Brunson] are going to carry us enough, so today obviously it was an all-around game. We’re always going to have their backs, and they always have ours, and it just shows you what type of team we are. It could be anybody on any night, but they’re going to carry us to the promised land.”

On Clarkson encouraging Pacôme Dadiet and reminding his teammates to stay ready:

“JC is always big on that, telling guys to stay ready. He was in [Dadiet’s] ear the whole shootaround [Wednesday morning]. Just telling everybody to stay ready because you never know when your name is called.”

On endorsing Tom Thibodeau as a potential head coaching hire for struggling NBA franchises:

“I made three playoffs with Thibodeau as my coach so his track record is one of success. So of course if I was a team that wanted to get back on track, I’d look at Tom Thibodeau to be my coach.”

On Thibodeau’s tactical knowledge, dedication and ability to prepare his teams to win:

“It’s the X’s and O’s and the amount of care he puts into his craft, his team. He steps into that gym every day and, you know, you can say anything you want about the way he coaches, but one thing I know is his team is prepared to win a game. So that’s a testament to who he is as a coach, the preparation he puts his team through and also his ability to have his team ready for the moment.”

On the Knicks’ bench players embracing fluctuating minutes and not having egos:

“We care about each other. We want to win for each other. We’re willing to take on different roles and we know that we’ve got each other’s back. If Jose’s got it going and my minutes are shortened, awesome. And vice versa. All of us, Deuce [McBride] included in that, I would throw him in that as well, all of us kind of feel that way. That’s really cool.

“I’ve been saying it, I’ve been a broken record about it, but you don’t see that — that’s very rare where no ego or ulterior motives get involved. That’s something special that you want to be a part of.”

items.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Heat, November 27, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
Back in the 1990s, one way to preserve basketball games for the future was to record them on a VHS cassette. For all the younger folks, this was a big, chunky, rectangular thing that had magnetic tape on the inside. Whenever a game was on TV, you popped your cassette into the video recorder, pressed “REC,” and from that point on, you could rewatch anything you recorded whenever you wanted. Or for as long as the tape held up, for that matter.

My favorite recorded event back then was Game Five of the first round of the playoffs in 1999 between your New York Knicks and the Miami Heat. It ended with Allan Houston’s historic leaning jumper with 0.8 seconds to go, sending the top-seeded team coached by the Godfather of Schenectady packing and the underdog Bockers on an improbable run all the way to the NBA Finals. The tape wasn’t just special to me because of the historic shot or the basketball played with bad intentions back then. It was also awesome because it showed the Knicks beating the Heat. Sorry, Grandma, I know you taught me not to hate anyone, but those were the Heat, my favorite team’s biggest rival for years.

Now, before A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend thinks he can hold a candle to the guy Patrick Ewing once offered one of his kidneys to, let me make it clear: That was a different time, a different rivalry. Whoever experienced it firsthand knows what I mean by that. When the Knicks meet the Heat on Friday night for their fourth NBA Cup game of the season, it will be different, much different. Different players, different coaches. Heck, it all seems like a different world. But make no mistake about it—it’s still Knicks versus Heat. Which means the stakes are just a bit higher than in a game versus the magicians from the nation’s capital or the royalty from “The Big Tomato.”

Knicks get first look at Giannis on the Heat

Friday’s game will be particularly interesting because it gives the Knicks a first glimpse at the newest version of the Heat, featuring Greece’s national hero Giannis Antetokounmpo, who also happens to be one of the greatest and probably most unique basketball players this generation has seen. The project started pretty badly, with Giannis continuously reminding everyone who cared and everyone who didn’t that he dearly missed Milwaukee, the city he had called home for every second of his storied NBA career until then. Then the schematic issues befell the not-so-hot Heat, who struggled with spacing, players playing in new roles, and the daunting task of implementing a headstrong player with immense gravity into a completely new system. Defense? Haha, good one!

But after a 3-6 start, the second-oldest team in the league decided this wasn’t the way to ride off into the sunset. Or rather, their famous coach made plenty of adjustments. Erik Spoelstra, as we all know, is one of the best in the business. Not only at taking average rosters into the Play-In Tournament but indeed at coaching that sport with the orange leather. He inserted young Pelle Larsson into the starting lineup, found a spacing solution for the Heat, doubled down on their identity as a full-court, offensive-minded team, and then watched his guys reel off seven mostly impressive victories in a row (among them wins over Houston and Detroit) before falling to Philly on Wednesday night.

What can we expect from the Heat specifically? They love to get up and down the court and play at the third-highest pace in the entire league. Currently, only the Memphis Grizzlies score more points than Spoelstra’s squad, and the Heat do it by shooting a high percentage from the field, drawing boatloads of fouls, and making use of two post players. Yes, you read that right—post players. Both Giannis and A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend can effectively score with their backs to the basket, and despite many worries, they can actually coexist next to one another. One of them fills the dunker spot almost all the time, they rotate decisively in screen actions, and overall, Miami runs its sets fast and ferociously to get them rolling downhill. They don’t just set screens to see where it leads them; they want to get into an action quickly before any lanes can close.

Heat, Spoelstra have adjusted after bad start

It works, partly because the players around Giannis and that guy who made a habit last year of disliking the team that won a championship before him are all doing a good job in their roles. Klay Thompson adds shooting (43.2 percent from downtown), Swedish Swiss Army knife Pelle Larsson provides a little bit of everything, and playmaker Davion Mitchell has all of a sudden turned into one of the better point guards in the league at age 28, averaging career highs of 17 points and 8.6 assists per contest while also shooting 51 percent from the floor and 43-plus percent from behind the arc. The bench has some older vets more or less collecting paychecks so far, but Bobby Portis and Andrew Wiggins clearly have some talent. Apparently, that also describes Ryan Conwell, a stocky second-round guard who has been a pleasant surprise for Miami.

That whole group will definitely look to waltz into Madison Square Garden on Friday with the idea of showing the champs that they are a team to be reckoned with. Whether they truly are remains to be seen; there are plenty of things that could uproot the positivity currently sprawling across South Beach. But the Knicks better be prepared for a tough test, and not because they might still be missing some of their injured guys or because they are coming off an emotionally draining victory against Cleveland on Wednesday. Not even because A’ja Wilson might have taught her boyfriend a few more tricks this offseason after winning her fifth WNBA MVP trophy.

No, it’s going to be tough because it’s Heat versus Knicks. And even if that doesn’t mean what it did in the days of the VHS cassette, it still means something.

items.title: Knicks 121, Cavaliers 102: “The most Mike Brown victory imaginable”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
It’s easy to get lost in today’s world. Everything is spinning so fast, so many things are out of control. Prices, taxes, wars, narratives, diabolical devices, our sense of togetherness. Life sometimes feels like an endless list of things that, no matter how much you scratch off, no matter what you decide not to worry about, gets longer by the minute. The NBA is no exception, a cutthroat world infected by influencing influences that expects daily reinvention, that wants to turn humans into brands and expand like a kraken gobbling up the last little dollars from the deepest pits of the coral reef.

As you watch another foul-baiting baller be rewarded for his deeds, followed by the 23rd commercial for guaranteed grifting, it can be tough to find the joy here from time to time, to remember why you ever thought this was fun. But then Jose Alvarado runs into the picture and steals a ball, only to rise up moments later for a three. He jumps for joy as he hits it, just like the little kid he once was on the playgrounds of the city that he now represents on the biggest stage there is in basketball. And you smile along with him.

Jose Alvarado carries the Knicks to victory

There is something inherently right about a guy like Jose Alvarado. Sure, he is an annoying pest defensively, loudmouthed, confident on his good days, cocky on his better ones. A guy you would probably hate if he wasn’t on your team. Not even in the fun way of hating an opponent, if there is one. No, you really can’t stand that little bugger, like, at all. Yet even if you root for some other franchise whose name doesn’t rhyme with clicks, deep down inside your basketball fan’s heart, you have to appreciate a guy, a man, a kid like Jose Alvarado. Mike Brown surely does.

It didn’t even take Alvarado’s tide-turning performance in the Knicks’ 121-102 destruction of the Cleveland Cavaliers in yesterday’s NBA Cup game, which was, as PolyphonicSpreewell so beautifully put it in the , “the most Mike Brown victory imaginable.” It didn’t take his 16 points in the fourth quarter or his 21 in total. But the light shining on Jose surely was a reminder that the big little Puerto Rican embodies what this New York basketball team is. Sure, they can beat you with Xs and Os, with the might of majestic superstars, with firepower that can put a New Year’s fireworks display to shame. But there is more that makes the Knicks the Knicks. A group that has a heart and a soul beyond what is expected of them, some inner power they can turn to when things go sideways. Something that lets them play and, more importantly, enjoy the game innocently, freely. How it was supposed to be experienced.

Alvarado is not your type of guy? , says Pacôme Djenon Dadiet! It didn’t matter that he didn’t really hit shots consistently yesterday or, frankly, ever before. He still plunged into the action versus the James Hardens and Donovan Mitchells of the world like the Knicks’ bench was a cliff and his name was Orlando Duque. Maybe not as gracefully, but definitely just as committed and energetic. And, most importantly, without any fear. There was no fear in Tyler Nickel, either, who at some point seemed as far away from real NBA minutes as his birthplace in the Shenandoah Valley is from Madison Square Garden. But don’t worry, bench guy, Mike Brown’s got a map, and he knows where to find you.

Mike Brown works his magic with the Knicks

With injuries to OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, plus ineffective and almost shockingly bad nights from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, the coach seemingly didn’t have to search yesterday. He just hurled everyone he had on his pine into the action and watched them stick it to the Cavs. Mo Diawara hit a three. James Wiseman dominated the paint for stretches in the fourth quarter. He didn’t look out of place; he didn’t look like he didn’t know what he was doing. Rather, he played like a man possessed, not by some evil power or the One Ring to rule them all, but by the unwavering confidence and belief of a bald, happy-go-lucky man who coaches champions.

These champions include a much-maligned Mikal Bridges, who carried the team throughout the entire second quarter. They also include Josh Hart and Landry Shamet, who did their thing and then some. They are all guys who had rough goes in the past but who never found themselves in Mr. Brown’s doghouse. They deserve to be singled out for pushing the ball in transition, for point-of-attack defense, for just being themselves. But frankly, who doesn’t? Everyone did a little and then a lot of what was needed from them. I’m sure Tyler Kolek was one of the biggest cheerleaders despite his rough night on the court. It all speaks to the culture that Mike Brown has bestowed upon this team, that he has created with all of his players. All of them. All these guys who know what hard work is. Who relish every opportunity they get.

And who have a way of playing basketball that is as much fun as you can imagine.

items.title: Knicks 121, Cavs 102: Scenes from a second-half bench bash
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks’ hopes of repeating as NBA Cup champions hinged on beating Cleveland (9-10) tonight and Miami on Friday, while Philadelphia had to beat Miami (which they did) and Indiana has to topple Philadelphia. Even then, advancement would come down to point differential, meaning New York (12-6) would likely need to win both games by double digits.

Consider the mission half completed. As you could deduce from the blazing blue court at Madison Square Garden, tonight’s tilt was a Cup game. Three Knicks were sidelined by injury: OG Anunoby, Miles McBride, and Jordan Clarkson. Anunoby’s absence was felt as the Cavaliers scored 61 first-half points (and a lopsided free-throw disparity stung, too). The adjustments Mike Brown made in the locker room paid dividends on the court. His squad applied stingier defense, got their turnovers under control, won the fourth quarter 39-17, and flipped the game to win, 121-102.

Of the six Knicks with double-digit points tonight, Jose Alvarado’s barrage of fourth-quarter triples and his season-high / team-high 21 were arguably the most impactful. On a short-handed night, and with multiple starters playing through injury, Jose was once again prepared to step into the spotlight and contribute meaningful minutes. What a professional! What depth!

Three consecutive turnovers didn’t help (two by Karl-Anthony Towns, one by Josh Hart) as the Knicks fell behind early in the first quarter. Midway through the period, Jalen Brunson scored seven in under two minutes to regain the lead. In this streaky contest, though, it made sense that he missed his next five attempts. Towns (12 PTS, 10 RBS, 7 AST, +21) was a game-time decision due to knee soreness, and his scoring showed the limp, producing a single point in the frame. Filling in for Anunoby in the first five, Landry Shamet made his sixth start of the season. He finished with a tidy 11 points on three made three-pointers.

The quarter was competitive until the final three minutes. After Pacôme Dadiet (yes, him!) drilled a triple to pull the Knicks within one, Cleveland rattled off a 10-0 run, powered by five consecutive points from Meleek Thomas, two Thomas Bryant free throws, and a Donovan Mitchell and-one. The latter easily had the biggest impact on the quarter, tallying 14 points, three dimes, and a steal. As for New York’s bench support, Dadiet (7 PTS, 14 MIN) provided positive defensive efforts with a block and a steal, but neither Tyler Kolek nor Andre Drummond moved the needle. New York managed just six points over the final five-ish minutes, and Cleveland closed the quarter ahead, 34-23.

To start the second, the good guys outscored the villains by ten, chiseling an 11-point deficit to one. Credit Towns and his four points, two dimes, and two blocks for the comeback. Mohamed Diawara lent a triple, too, and Mikal Bridges found his rhythm, blasting out seven fast points. Naturally, Cleveland responded with a 9-2 stretch when James Harden (28 PTS, 1-8 3PT) finally got on the board. Dadiet drizzled water on our good feelings by missing three straight shots, and Brunson still couldn’t regain his touch, going scoreless from the field in the period.

Playing from 55-44 down with four minutes left in the half, the hosts posted 11 unanswered points, eight of which belonged to Bridges. He’d finish the half with 17 points. This, my friends, is what’s known as a :

Despite dealing with a sore shoulder, Hart picked Harden’s pocket twice, converting one steal into a layup. Unfortunately, after Bridges tied the game at 55, Donovan Mitchell (30 PTS, 1-7 3PT) and Harden combined for six unanswered points, aided by a Bridges turnover. The home team won the quarter 33-27 but entered intermission trailing 61-56.

Through the half, Harden and Mitchell combined for 34 points in the half, while their bench contributed 13. New York had shot better from the field (54% to 49%) and significantly better from deep (50% to 31%), they were on the wrong end of the score due to a glaring free-throw disparity. New York had attempted just eight freebies, while Cleveland shot more than twice that. The Cavs outscored won the paint, 28-16, and the boards. Another glaring stat: Cleveland converted six Knicks miscues into 13 points, while New York squeezed just two points out of five giveaways.

Cleveland opened the second half on an 11-5 run to restore its double-digit lead. Down 74-65 midway through the period, the Knicks got a boost from an unexpected source: Tyler Nickel. The rookie sank a triple, followed by another from Landry Shamet, to cut the deficit to three. Nickel contributed five points but also committed four fouls in under six minutes—that will get straightened out with experience. Harden extended Cleveland’s advantage to 85-77 with under three minutes remaining. But then another unexpected player pitched in: James Wiseman provided some valuable minutes off the bench, finishing the game with six points and seven boards in six minutes. Shamet helped the Knicks win the quarter 26-24 and enter the fourth trailing 85-82.

The Knicks opened the fourth quarter on a 12-0 run, turning a three-point deficit into a nine-point advantage in less than three minutes. Jose Alvarado (a team-high 21 points, 8-10 FG, 19 MIN) was the catalyst, drilling consecutive triples and picking Donovan Mitchell’s pocket to set up a Dadiet layup. Hart took a turn orchestrating the offense, collecting four assists during the opening surge. The Ohio Players missed their first five shots, four of them by Mitchell, and committed two turnovers as the Knicks piled on the points.

Wiseman (!) helped goose New York’s lead to 13 with four points and three offensive rebounds in a brief fourth-quarter stint. When Mitchell and Harden scored five unanswered points to trim the deficit to eight, Alvarado responded with a jumper, and Jalen Brunson buried a triple, his only basket of the quarter. Alvarado was the unquestionable star of the fourth, scoring 16 of his 21 points, including four three-pointers. Hart was nearly as impactful, contributing eight points, six assists, three rebounds, a steal, and a block in the frame. The Knicks closed on a 7-0 run, their defense holding Cleveland scoreless over the final two minutes and change.

Welcome back to associate head coach Chris Jent, who returned to the sidelines after a month away.

The Knicks hang around town to face the Heat on Friday in the last of their first-stage Cup games. Mo is folding and pressing your recap. Happy Knicksgiving, turkey fans.

items.title: Landry Shamet has arrived. Why can’t he be Sixth Man of the Year?
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Chicken Littles can relax. Our world champion Knicks are 11–6, sit fourth in the Eastern Conference, and have won eight of their last 10 games, including five straight. Karl-Anthony Towns is having an MVP-caliber season, and Captain Jalen Brunson is warming up after a short, celebration-heavy offseason. Another player who’s getting some buzz isn’t one of the starters, but the team’s sharpest weapon off the bench.

When asked about Landry Shamet’s play this season, head coach Mike Brown said the 6’5” guard “should be Sixth Man of the Year. It’s not close.” Mike should know. He has a front-row seat to the Shamet show every night and at every practice.

One stat I take note of is Game Score. John Hollinger designed it to measure a player’s box-score production in a single game. Game Score uses a scale that roughly resembles points scored, with 10 considered an average performance and 40 an outstanding one. It rewards scoring, made field goals, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks. Shot attempts, missed free throws, turnovers, and personal fouls subtract from the total, and offensive rebounds count more than defensive rebounds.

Through 17 games, Shamet has averaged a Game Score of 8.24. That puts him fourth on the team behind Towns (19.83), Brunson (18.66), and OG Anunoby (11.57). Two starters, Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, rank fifth and sixth at 6.35 and 5.94, respectively.

This season has been a coming out party for Landry. Although primarily a linchpin of the second unit, he has filled in for starters five times this campaign and is averaging 26.9 minutes per game, the second-most of his NBA career. Consider these statistics, all career-best:

  • A shade under 50% from the field
  • 65% effective field goal percentage
  • Eight field goal attempts per game
  • 5.6 triples tried per game
  • 11.4 points per game, fourth-best on the team

The only Knick shooting better from deep is Jordan Clarkson (50%), coincidentally the 2020–21 Sixth Man of the Year. And Jordan’s attempted only 12 longballs.

When Hart and Bridges have struggled to find the net, plenty of people have beaten the drum for Shamet to replace one of them in the first five. That sounds fine in theory, but consider Mike Brown’s perspective. First, there’s the harmony of keeping the Villanova brethren together, and who knows what effect a “demotion” for Josh or Kal might have on the locker room? Second, Shamet is Mike’s security blanket. If the starters are spinning their wheels, nothing injects energy into the festivities like a Landry pull-up three on the move. The MSG crowd explodes, and you can see his teammates quicken with excitement. Furthermore, Shamet is doing much of his damage against the opponent’s backups. That’s hardly a fair fight. AND when the score is close and the team needs a bucket, Brown can turn to Captain Clutch, Towns, and his sparkplug Shamet. Even if Landry doesn’t start, he sure can finish.

One downer about Landry’s success is the ripple effect on the roster. Overshadowed by Shamet’s sizzling shooting is the fact that Miles McBride is also shooting a career high from downtown (42%). Deuce was once a first-off-the-bench candidate. Now, with Shamet hitting the three-ball and Tyler Kolek coming into his own as a playmaker (averaging 4.1 assists to 0.6 turnovers in 13.3 minutes per game), McBride is down to 17.2 minutes per night, the fourth-highest average of his six-season career. Meanwhile, the Knicks find themselves dreadfully thin at center, with Andre Drummond losing the plot around the 10-minute mark most nights and James Wiseman yet to prove he can hang. Shamet + Kolek + Drummond + Wiseman = an expendable Deuce. No one here will be surprised if McBride, the longest-tenured Knick, is traded before the deadline for a serviceable big man. No, we won’t like it, but we’ll understand it.

Consider this: only three Knicks have won Sixth Man of the Year.

    Why can’t ShamWow be the fourth? He’ll have some stiff competition in the race. Boston’s Payton Pritchard is the current betting favorite for Sixth Man of the Year (+160 at BetMGM). That vanilla Milk Dud averages 13.7 points per game. Other top contenders include Ajay Mitchell (Thunder), Dylan Harper (Spurs), Jrue Holiday (Blazers), and Ayo Dosunmu (Timberwolves). Jared McCain and Daniss Jenkins are dark horses.

    The stats make Landry a strong candidate, though. Through Nov. 22, Shamet ranked fifth in the NBA in on/off net rating among 242 qualifying players on HoopsNightly’s leaderboard. The Knicks outscored opponents by 17.2 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and were outscored by 8.3 with him off it. That’s a swing of +25.5. (KnickStats gives him an even better number, +28.)

    There used to be two knocks on Shamet, now in his ninth season. The first was that his defense stunk. Well, whattayaknow: according to KnickStats, the Knicks have allowed 101.3 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and 117.5 with him off it. The other concern was the injury bug. He’s missed significant time with lower-body issues, including multiple ankle sprains, a foot injury that kept him out for an extended stretch in 2023, and a calf strain that ended his 2023–24 season. Then came the right-shoulder setbacks, a dislocation in the 2024 preseason and a sprain in 2025 that sidelined him for roughly a month. For now (no jinxes), he’s been the picture of health, playing every game of the campaign (we all wince whenever he smashes to the floor).

    Everything’s good until it isn’t again. So it goes. For now, the Knicks are surging and tonight they’ll face a familiar rival in the Cleveland Cavaliers. If you saw the injury report, it’s a little dicey. Anunoby and Clarkson are out, while Hart, McBride, and Towns are all game-time decisions. That’s a concerning list at first blush, but with sixth man Shamet in their back pocket, the Knicks still have a good chance to win their sixth straight. What a time to be a fan.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘No excuses’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Isn’t it crazy that nearly a fifth of the Knicks’ regular-season games after tonight’s matchup would have been played against the same opponent in the Cavs?

Well, that’s true, and so is that New York is about to beat Cleveland to take a 2-1 series lead, won’t it?

Here’s a damn whole lot of quotes to keep you entertained before tipoff.

On the inconsistency of the media’s coverage and criticism of Mikal Bridges:

“Yes. Yes. But that’s your guys’ [the media] job; that’s why you guys get paid. You guys get paid to question and embellish and some other things. We understand that; we know it. You’re looking for stories; we know it.”

On Cleveland’s physicality and what the Knicks must improve in their third meeting Wednesday:

“They were real physical in Game 2. You give them credit. They talked about keeping us off the glass and some other things, and they did it. They’re a great-coached team with Kenny Atkinson and a great team in general.

“There’s gonna have to be a lot of things that we do better in this game, starting with the level of physicality, while getting out in transition, if we expect to get a win.”

On using Jose Alvarado alongside Jalen Brunson to relieve defensive pressure:

“To be able to get (Brunson) off the ball and let somebody else handle the pressure has been huge for us. And also, it gives (Brunson’s) defender a different rhythm, as opposed to being on the ball from the start to the end. You can get in a certain rhythm and get locked in pretty good with it. It can be to your advantage, but if he’s on the ball, then off the ball, then back on the ball, that’s a little harder to adjust to.”

On drawing inspiration from how Golden State deployed Stephen Curry:

“I’m not comparing the players at all in terms of their game, but when I was in Golden State, we used Steph (Curry this way). He was on the ball, then he was off the ball, and to have to make that adjustment throughout the course of the game, not just once or twice but multiple times, is huge. And Jose gives us that ability, because he can guard certain players on the other team, and then if you wanna pressure him, he’s been in that position before. He’ll go by you and sometimes still execute our offense, but he can go by you and make you pay with sprays.”

On his preseason conversation with Jose Alvarado and Tyler Kolek about competing for minutes:

“I said, ‘Hey, right now, Jose, it’s your job because you finished the season that way and you both helped us win at a high level.’ ‘Tyler, you helped us win the NBA Cup and Jose, you helped us win in the finals.’ And I said you guys are really close and it may be you, Jose, for seven games and then it could be Tyler for three, so it’s going to be a competition you have to be ready for the entire year.”

On Alvarado’s defensive advantages over Kolek and the latter’s development:

“Jose Alvarado gives us that ability because he can guard certain players on the other team. And then if you want to pressure him he’s been in that position before, he’ll go by you and sometimes still execute our offense, but he can go by you and make you pay with sprays.

“Tyler Kolek has been getting better on the defensive end of the floor. He’s improved a lot and he’s going to continue to improve as a young guy but Jose has been in the league longer and he knows the league, a little quicker. Teams don’t try and attack him in an iso situation because, as quick as he is, if you mess around with the ball too much he may get a steal and go the other way with it.”

On the Alvarado-Brunson pairing not being exclusively reserved for closing games:

“Well it’s not closing moments. It’s just throughout the course of the ballgame, it’s slotted on my minute sheet and if you think back, the probably best game that comes to mind is in Indiana. Even in the first [of two games last week] in Toronto teams are picking up trying to wear him down and so to be able to get him off the ball and let somebody else handle pressure has been huge for us.

“Also, it gives his defender a different rhythm as opposed to being on the ball from the start to the end. You can get in a certain rhythm and get locked in pretty good with it and it can be to your advantage but if he’s on the ball then off the ball then back on the ball that’s a little harder to adjust to.”

On Josh Hart’s triple-double and defensive performance against Indiana:

“Josh, triple-double. He was really good tonight on both ends of the floor. He was our defensive player of the game, so just a whale of a game for him.”

On Landry Shamet’s season to date:

“He should be sixth man of the year. It’s not even close.”

On identifying with Knicks fans:

“I always see myself in the fans. I look in the crowd, and I see 19,000 people that look just like me.”

On Knicks fans pulling over on the highway in the Hamptons to take pictures with him:

“I was just with my family. I forgot what we were doing. We were doing something and it was, like, three, four or five cars that’s driving, pulling over to ask for photos. I’m like, bro, I ain’t one of these [superstars]. I ain’t KD. I ain’t Bron. I ain’t Steph. But for that it was funny because I’m just like, that shows you the love and the appreciation that New York Knicks fans have, to be on the highway and pull over and ask me for a photo. Whether you’re in New York, the Hamptons or any vacation spot that real New Yorkers go to, you get the love and the appreciation. It’s cool because you’re able to see what the actual heartbeat of the Garden is.”

On the image that comes to mind when thinking about hardworking New Yorkers:

On seeing his own sacrifices and work ethic reflected in Knicks fans:

“When people ask me about it, I always say I see myself in the fans because at the end of the day, well, yeah, I’m probably a little more athletic than they are, a little more gifted in terms of basketball than they are, but New York is hard work. It’s a lot of countless hours, a lot of loss, you know, losing sleep, a lot of sacrifice. And I feel like it’s the same in my shoes, and that’s when I go out and play as hard as I can, because I look in the crowd and I see 19,000 people that look just like me. I think that’s what New Yorkers look like.”

On finding consistency in New York under Tom Thibodeau:

“I felt like I had moments in L.A. and New Orleans and Portland. But I feel like once I got to New York, starting with Thibs, it was a constant.”

On his unpredictable playing style and approaching NBA games like playground basketball:

“I feel like sometimes that’s why a scouting report might be tough for someone like me because it’s just, like, you don’t know what he’s gonna do this day. You don’t know if he might hit four or five threes today or he might have 2 points but 15 rebounds or he might have 6, 7 assists. If you go to a park right now and you just see a kid playing and just doing random stuff, that’s JHart, and that’s how I look at it when I step on the court. I look back to when I’m playing in the playground, I’m just doing random stuff. But it’s random stuff within somewhat of a structure.”

On prioritizing his teammates’ success over his own:

“I don’t really play the game for praise or anything like that. I’ll leave that. I want JB to get his flowers, KAT, Kal, OG, Deuce, Lan. I want those guys to get their flowers, and if I get it, cool. But that’s more important to me, seeing those guys get the accolades that they want, the contracts that they want, the money that they want, the notoriety that they want. And if they get that and I don’t get any, I’m cool with it. So I don’t know, I just… I feel like it changed. I feel like before, you know, you wanted the glitz and the glamour about it, but I don’t know. It’s not really in my heart anymore.”

On unrealistic expectations surrounding Bridges because of the Knicks’ trade package:

“Everyone looks at the trade package and they expect him to be like a No. 2 guy, No. 3 guy, but that’s not what is asked of him to do. He was a guy who was the No. 1 option in Brooklyn. I’m not sure what it was, but I’m sure he was probably averaging around 20 [points per game] or close to it. We got him and we basically asked him to take a smaller role. So you’re not necessarily gonna get the production of a 1A guy being the fourth option, the fifth option at times.”

On Bridges sacrificing individual production for the team’s success:

“I think it’s unfair in that regard, because he could do more, and I’m sure at times he wants to do more, but he’s willing to sacrifice and put the team in front of himself, which we commend him for. … His role could be bigger. I’m sure he at times would like it to be bigger. But he never says anything about it, he never mopes around about it. He just does what is asked of him to do and he tries to do it to the best of his ability.”

On passing up easy baskets to give others scoring opportunities:

“I don’t play the game for stats. I just saw an open man in front of me. Kind of the same thing in Toronto where it was a bobbled play; I could have went and got a dunk and tried to get going offensively. But see a guy in front of me, I’m going to pass it.”

On Brunson returning a pass to help him overcome his physical and mental struggles during recent games

“Oh yeah, for sure. That shows, obviously, he knows I’ve been struggling a little bit physically and mentally and trying to figure it out and trying to get there, that was one of the things, get that pass, get an easy two points, see the ball go through and then play.”

On climbing the Knicks’ all-time triple-double leaderboard and late improvement:

“I don’t know. It feels good to be stacking up some good games. I feel like the last couple games have been better. I have been knocking down shots, but the quality of my play has been better. Obviously, it feels good to have three games in a row that have been better. It feels good that I continue to stack them.”

On dealing with a lingering injury to his shooting shoulder:

“A lot of things are going on with my shoulder. It’s been barking for a couple weeks. So now, we got a couple days where we can figure some stuff out within the couple-day break and hopefully get it feeling better.”

On whether Taylor Swift is welcome at Madison Square Garden:

“Obviously. I can’t believe I have to say this. But I didn’t say what was said. Being one of the leaders of the team — the captain of the team — I guess I now have to help somebody out. Yes, she’s a member of the Knicks fandom. Yes, she is.”

On outside narratives surrounding Bridges and his work ethic:

“Everyone outside this organization has their own narrative or belief in things that we can do as a team or players can do individually. But that’s just their own narrative. … He’s one of the hardest workers we have and that won’t change.”

On Bridges’ ability to deliver in high-pressure situations:

“We’ve seen what he does when the lights are the brightest. He steps up to the plate. Mikal’s one of those guys, when you have him in the locker room, when he’s on your team, you feel really good about your odds.”

On what makes Alvarado such a difficult opponent:

“It’s annoying. Any person on the other team will tell you the same thing. He’s a pest. Obviously, you see him shooting the ball really well these last two games. When he’s bringing his whole arsenal to the game, he’s a dangerous player for any team.”

On Bridges’ character, work ethic and ability to handle outside criticism:

“He’s one of the best people I know. I get the pleasure of seeing him every day and seeing how he works. Knowing that any good and bad stretch in the NBA can change very quickly, he’s always in a position to put himself in a good position and keep himself there. He knows what he’s capable of, I know what he’s capable of, and he’s always gonna do the right thing, take care of his teammates and take care of the work on his end, which is to keep fighting, regardless of noise — and there’s a lot of it that he has to deal with. He does a hell of a job.”

On repeatedly rewatching Game 4 of the NBA Finals throughout the summer:

“It obviously made it 10 times better that I was a part of it. But that was my favorite game watching as a fan.”

On not considering himself a small guard and earning Brown’s defensive trust:

“(I) don’t play like that. I think Mike believes in me defensively and understands that I can definitely play a bigger point guard role.”

On the Knicks’ mutual trust despite competition for playing time:

“Yeah, I mean we just trust everybody on the roster. You never know when your number is going to be called, so we just got to be ready. And we’re big on that, you know, just trust each other, and whoever is out there, we believe they’re going to win the game.

“I mean, it showed from last year. If you look at how we celebrated when we were winning and you know certain people, certain roles, were doing what they were supposed to do and we just had to cheer them on — genuinely. We really care about each other, and we know whoever’s name is out there, we’re going to just believe in whoever is out there and win the game.”
